title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
description: Brute force to optimized: restarting the scan from every start versus a single coordinated variable-size sliding window that jumps left using last-seen positions.

blocks.text: Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring without any repeating characters.

blocks.caption: Grow the window; on hitting a repeat, jump left straight past its last occurrence

blocks.text: Given a string s, find the length of the longest contiguous substring that contains no character more than once.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Growing Guest List With No Repeats Allowed
blocks.text: Like admitting guests one at a time into a room that can never have two guests with the same name. The moment a repeat name shows up, everyone admitted before (and including) that name's previous entry must effectively leave first, and admission continues from just after that point.

blocks.caption: Remembering last positions lets the window jump left in one step instead of crawling

blocks.text: Before restarting the scan from every possible starting position, notice that once a repeated character is found, exactly how far left to jump can be computed instantly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The condition "no repeated characters" is a property of the whole window, and a repeat anywhere inside it invalidates the entire window from that point backward.

Observation 2: Tracking the LAST index each character was seen at lets a repeat be detected in O(1), without scanning the window's contents.

Observation 3: When a repeat is found, the window doesn't need to shrink one step at a time. It can jump left directly to just past the repeated character's previous occurrence, as long as that occurrence is still within the current window (not from an already-invalidated stretch).

Observation 4: Track the maximum window length (right - left + 1) seen throughout this single coordinated pass.

Recognizing that a hash map of last-seen positions turns "find where to shrink to" into an O(1) lookup, instead of a step-by-step crawl, is the key optimization here.
This is the variable-size sliding window pattern, specialized with a "jump left directly" shrink instead of a one-step-at-a-time shrink, made possible by tracking last-seen positions.
For every possible starting position, extend forward using a set until a repeat is found.

items: For every possible starting position, walk forward, adding characters to a set, stopping the moment a character already in the set would be added again.
Track the length of the longest such stretch found across every starting position.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A fresh set is built for every starting position, since each independent walk needs to track its own repeat-free stretch.
The inner walk stops the moment a repeat is detected, since continuing further from this same start could never help.
best only ever increases, tracking the single longest repeat-free stretch found across every starting position.

blocks.text: Every possible starting position is checked directly, walking forward until a repeat is found, so the correct maximum is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) in the worst case, since each of the n starting positions can walk forward up to n characters.
Space: O(min(n, alphabet size)) for the set at any given walk.

Limitation: restarting the set from scratch at every new starting position ignores that a single coordinated window, combined with last-seen-position tracking, can jump directly to the correct new starting point instead of re-walking character by character.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force restarts its scan from scratch at every starting position. Instead, maintain a single window and a hash map of each character's last-seen index. Grow the window from the right. When a character is seen again, check whether its last occurrence still falls within the current window; if so, jump left directly to just past that occurrence, in a single O(1) step rather than shrinking one position at a time. Update the last-seen index for every character processed, and track the maximum window length throughout.

Maintain a window with a left and right boundary, along with a hash map from character to its most recent index. Grow the window by advancing right. When the current character was last seen at or after left, jump left directly to one past that last-seen index. Track the maximum window length seen throughout.
Grow the window from the right, jumping left directly whenever a repeat within the current window is found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since right advances exactly n times and left only ever moves forward, never resetting.
Space: O(min(n, alphabet size)) for the last-seen hash map.

The last-seen map always holds each character's most recent index seen so far, anywhere in s (not just within the current window). Checking that this last-seen index is at or after left confirms the repeat is genuinely inside the current window (a stale last-seen index from before left simply gets ignored), letting the window jump left directly to the correct new position in one step, rather than needing to crawl forward one element at a time.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Character not seen before, or last seen before left","No repeat within the window; keep growing"],["Character last seen at or after left","A genuine repeat within the window; jump left to one past that last-seen index"]]}

items: The `>= left` check is essential, since a character's last-seen index might be stale (from before the current window began) and should not trigger an unnecessary jump.
last_seen is updated for every character processed, whether or not it triggered a jump, always reflecting the most recent index seen.
best is updated after any needed jump, always reflecting the currently valid window's true length.

blocks.text: Tracking each character's last-seen index turns "find the correct new left boundary" from a step-by-step crawl into an O(1) direct jump, a technique reusable whenever a window's invalidating condition depends on a specific past position rather than an aggregate count.

items: Shrinking the window one position at a time on a repeat instead of jumping directly to one past the repeat's last-seen index.
Forgetting the `>= left` staleness check, which can cause an incorrect jump backward using an outdated last-seen index from before the current window.
Not updating the last-seen index for every character, including ones that didn't trigger a jump.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["s is empty","The answer is 0, since there are no characters at all"],["s has all distinct characters","The answer is s.length, since the entire string is already repeat-free"],["s has all identical characters","The answer is 1, since any 2-character stretch would repeat"]]}

items: Explicitly justify the `>= left` staleness check when explaining the solution, since it's the subtle detail that most easily gets missed or hand-waved.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Longest substring/subarray without a repeated element" points toward a variable-size sliding window using a last-seen-position map, allowing the left boundary to jump directly rather than crawl.

items: How would you also report the actual substring, not just its length? Track the left and right boundaries at the moment best is updated, then slice s using those indices.
What if the alphabet were small and fixed (say, only lowercase letters)? A fixed-size array of 26 last-seen indices could replace the hash map, trading flexibility for a smaller constant factor.

How would this change if you needed the longest substring with AT MOST k repeated characters allowed? This becomes a frequency-count-based variable-size window, similar in spirit to Longest Repeating Character Replacement.

A variable-size sliding window, in the same family as Longest Repeating Character Replacement and Fruit Into Baskets, but using a last-seen-position jump instead of a frequency-map-based incremental shrink.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(min(n, alphabet size)) space.
Optimized (variable-size sliding window with last-seen jump): O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet size)) space.

items: Pattern: Variable-size sliding window with a last-seen-position hash map, jumping left directly on a repeat
Core Idea: Track each character's last-seen index; on a genuine repeat inside the window, jump left to one past that position instead of crawling
Time: O(n)
Space: O(min(n, alphabet size))
Most Important Observation: A hash map of last-seen positions turns "where to shrink to" into an O(1) direct jump instead of a step-by-step crawl
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: On a repeat, jump left to just past its last-seen index
